evidence.title: Taymāʾ Oasis (NW Saudi Arabia): Qaryyah compound, walls & Neo-Babylonian King Nabonidus's 10-year residence
evidence.summary: Surrounded by multi-kilometre stone ramparts guarding artesian groundwater, Taymāʾ thrived at the junction of the Incense Road and Mesopotamia. Between 552 and 543 BCE the Neo-Babylonian King Nabonidus made Taymāʾ his royal desert residence (attested on the Harran stelae and local Taymāʾ cuneiform/Taymanitic rock texts), followed by Lihyanite and Nabataean eras.
evidence.limits: Excavations reveal Bronze Age walls much earlier than Iron Age Nabonidus; local political control alternated with northern oasis leagues.
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon-dated compound levels, Taymanitic inscriptions, and Neo-Babylonian royal chronicle correlations.

evidence.title: Dadān / al-Khuraybah (Al-ʿUlā, Saudi Arabia): Dadanite & Lihyanite monumental capitals
evidence.summary: Capital of the ancient kingdoms of Dadan and Lihyan centuries before Nabataean Hegra, al-Khuraybah featured a monumental sanctuary precinct with sacred lustration basin, sandstone royal colossi exceeding two metres in height, rock-cut lion tombs, and hundreds of Dadanitic script inscriptions documenting caravan tithes and Minaean merchant colonies.
evidence.limits: Relative chronological sequence separating early Dadan and Lihyan dynasties rests on royal epigraphy and pottery stratigraphy still undergoing active revision.
evidence.dateBasis: Dadanitic royal inscriptions and stratified pottery collections from Jabal Dādān / al-Khuraybah.

evidence.title: Dūmat al-Jandal / Adummatu (al-Jawf, Saudi Arabia): oasis queens, fortified ramparts & Mosque of ʿUmar
evidence.summary: Described in Neo-Assyrian annals (8th–7th c. BCE) as *Adummatu*—the desert stronghold of the Arab Queens Zabibe, Samsi, Te'elhunu, and Tabua raided by Sennacherib and Esarhaddon—Dūmat al-Jandal controlled the direct Wadi Sirhan caravan axis between Arabia and Syria through Nabataean, Roman (Mārid Castle), and early Islamic times.
evidence.limits: Ramparts at Dūmat al-Jandal show multi-phase Bronze-to-Islamic rebuilding; association between every Assyrian-named queen and specific excavated rooms is circumstantial.
evidence.dateBasis: Assyrian annal synchronisms, Nabataean–Roman inscriptions, and oasis wall radiocarbon chronology.

evidence.title: Maʾrib & Ṣirwāḥ (Kingdom of Sabaʾ, Yemen): Great Dam, Awām Temple & Sabaean epigraphy
evidence.summary: Anchor of the ancient South Arabian Kingdom of Sabaʾ, the engineered stone sluices of the Great Dam of Maʾrib harnessed monsoon wadi flash floods to irrigate nearly 10,000 hectares of oasis fields, funding monumental Sabaean sanctuaries (Barʾān and Awām/*Maḥram Bilqīs*), long bronze-and-limestone state inscriptions (*Karibʾīl Watar* c. 685 BCE), and the overland frankincense trunk route north to Gaza and Mesopotamia.
evidence.limits: Modern geopolitical conflict prevents continuous conservation; early first-millennium BCE high vs. short Sabaean chronologies remain refined within ~100 years.
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO World Heritage property stratigraphy, radiocarbon sediment dating, and royal Sabaean epigraphy.

evidence.title: Qaryat al-Fāw (Edge of Empty Quarter, Saudi Arabia): caravan city of Kinda & Old Arabic
evidence.summary: Guarding the solitary canyon pass through the Tuwaiq Escarpment between Najran and Eastern Arabia, UNESCO-listed Qaryat al-Fāw thrived as a planned fortified market town, temple quarter, and capital of Ma'add/Kinda—yielding Hellenistic-influenced bronzes, colorful frescoes, stone incense burners, and the famous 1st-c. BCE/CE Sabaic-script Old Arabic funerary inscription of Mu'awiyah ibn Rabi'ah.
evidence.limits: Abandoned abruptly around the 5th century CE as regional caravan corridors and climatic water tables shifted.
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO inscription dossier, Hellenistic–Roman glass/bronze typologies, and Old Arabic/Musnad epigraphy.

evidence.title: Thāj, Gerrha & Tylos (Eastern Province, Saudi Arabia & Bahrain): Gulf caravan & pearl trading ports
evidence.summary: Linked to Classical descriptions of wealthy *Gerrha* (a city of salt-crust houses trading Arabian incense, Indian spices, and Gulf pearls by caravan across central Arabia to Petra and Seleucid Mesopotamia), the walled ashlar settlement at Thāj yielded 3rd-c. BCE Hasaean inscriptions, Seleucid-weight silver coinage, and a celebrated royal child burial wearing a gold funerary mask and pearl-gold jewelry.
evidence.limits: Whether ancient Gerrha stood squarely at Thāj, Uqair, or al-Jubayl remains actively researched.
evidence.dateBasis: Selective Hellenistic Attic/Seleucid ceramic & coin horizons, Hasaean texts, and ashlar stratigraphy.

evidence.title: Salūt, Aflāj Canals & Sumhuram (Oman): subterranean hydrology & Dhofar frankincense harbor
evidence.summary: Iron Age communities across northern Oman engineered *aflāj* underground gravity galleries tapping piedmont aquifers alongside fortified hill complexes like Salūt, while southern Hadramawt founded the fortified coastal depot of Sumhuram (Khor Rori) in Dhofar around the late 1st century BCE to ship Boswellia sacra frankincense to Roman Red Sea harbors and Gujarat.
evidence.limits: Radiocarbon and OSL dating places Oman's earliest documented falaj galleries around the early first millennium BCE alongside Bronze Age agricultural continuity.
evidence.dateBasis: Quaternary geoarchaeology at Salut oasis and UNESCO Aflāj / Land of Frankincense inscriptions.

evidence.title: Hegra / Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ (Al-Ḥijr, Saudi Arabia): Nabataean caravan metropolis & Roman southern frontier
evidence.summary: Nabataea's second capital after Petra, UNESCO-listed Hegra preserves 111 carved sandstone tomb facades (dated 1 BCE–75 CE by Nabataean legal inscriptions), hundreds of rock-cut wells and catchment dams, residential mud-brick quarters, a 175–177 CE Latin inscription of Rome's Legio III Cyrenaica, and the 267/356 CE Raqosh tomb inscription documenting the transition into early Arabic epigraphy.
evidence.limits: Many sandstone cliff tombs belong to wealthy Nabataean officers and matrons while ordinary mud-brick townsfolk lived inside the enclosed oasis plain.
evidence.dateBasis: Precisely dated Nabataean regnal facade inscriptions, Roman Latin military epigraphy, and residential excavations.

evidence.title: Zafār & Ḥimā Cultural Area (Himyarite & Najrān Corridor): highland unification & dated pre-Islamic rock texts
evidence.summary: From 110 BCE onward, the Himyarite calendar marked an indigenous highland state at Zafār (Yemen) that absorbed Sabaʾ and Hadramawt around 275–300 CE, officially embracing strict monotheism (*Rahmānan*) by the late 4th century. Just north along the caravan bottleneck of Najrān, UNESCO's Ḥimā Cultural Area records thousands of Old South Arabian, Thamudic, Christian, Jewish, and 518/523 CE Himyarite–Abraha royal campaign inscriptions.
evidence.limits: Hima rock panels span millennia from hunting scenes to dated 6th-century military marches.
evidence.dateBasis: Himyarite calendar-dated royal inscriptions (Murayghan & Bir Hima) verified on UNESCO WHC dossiers.

evidence.title: Jubbah, Shuwaymis & Early Arabic Epigraphy (Ḥāʾil–Khaybar): desert literacy across the Hijaz & Najd
evidence.summary: Beyond ancient rock art along extinct paleolakes at UNESCO-listed Jubbah and Shuwaymis, pastoralists and oasis dwellers engraved tens of thousands of Thamudic, Safaitic, Hismaic, and late Nabataean-to-Paleo-Arabic texts across northern Arabia's basalt *ḥarrāt*, demonstrating widespread pastoral literacy, tribal genealogies, weather prayers, and the evolutionary script bridge to classical Arabic.
evidence.limits: Coordinate marks the Jubbah oasis basin; pastoral epigraphic concentrations stretch across Hail, Khaybar, and Jordan's black basalt desert.
evidence.dateBasis: Palaeographic script evolution and associated Khaybar–Jubbah oasis geoarchaeology.

evidence.title: Darb Zubaydah & al-Rabadhah (Kufa–Mecca Pilgrim Road): Abbasid desert engineering (c. 750–1000 CE)
evidence.summary: Extending ~1,400 km from Kufa across waterless Najdi gravel plains to Mecca and Medina, the Darb Zubaydah was fitted out with over 50 stepped masonry rainwater cisterns (*birak*), wells, milestones, mosques, and fortified waystations—especially through endowments organized by Abbasid queen Zubaydah bint Ja'far (d. 831 CE), turning Najd into a permanently watered highway corridor centered around towns like al-Rabadhah.
evidence.limits: Sections were damaged after Qarmatian raids in the 10th century though key cisterns remained in seasonal nomadic use into early modern times.
evidence.dateBasis: Early Islamic Kufic road milestones, Umayyad/Abbasid hydraulic survey masonry, and excavated towns like al-Rabadhah.

evidence.title: Historic Jeddah / al-Balad (Red Sea Coast, Saudi Arabia): Red Sea spice harbor & Gate to Makkah (647–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Designated in 647 CE by Caliph ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān as Mecca's principal sea harbor replacing older al-Shuʿaybah, Historic Jeddah grew under Rasulid, Mamluk, Sharifian, and Ottoman governance into a cosmopolitan Indian Ocean–Red Sea entrepôt whose fossil-coral masonry tower houses with shaded cedar *rawāshīn* wooden lattices sheltered pilgrims and merchants from East Africa to Indonesia.
evidence.limits: Surviving multi-storey timber-and-coral houses date mainly to the 18th–late 19th centuries resting over deeper Islamic urban strata.
evidence.dateBasis: 647 CE Caliph ʿUthmān port establishment chronicle, Mamluk fortification wall (1517 CE), and UNESCO heritage corpus.

evidence.title: Damascus (Syria): Umayyad Caliphate capital, Great Mosque & Ottoman Hajj marshaling city (661–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Capital of the Umayyad Caliphate (661–750 CE) stretching from Iberia to Sindh, Damascus transformed the Roman precinct of Jupiter Damascenus/St. John the Baptist into Caliph al-Walīd I's Great Mosque (706–715 CE), later thriving under Nur al-Din Zangi, Saladin's Ayyubids, the Mamluks, and as the annual Ottoman military and caravan assembly point (*Mahmal*) for the Syrian Hajj route to Medina and Mecca.
evidence.limits: Living historic city preserving Roman grid bones beneath Medieval and Ottoman bazaars and khans.
evidence.dateBasis: Umayyad dynastic foundation (661 CE), Mosque foundation epigraphy (706 CE), and Ottoman Hajj registers.

evidence.title: Jerusalem / al-Quds: First/Second Temple masonry, Constantine's Church, Dome of the Rock & Ottoman walls
evidence.summary: At the spiritual intersection of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, Jerusalem preserves First Temple Iron Age water works (Siloam Tunnel), Herodian Temple Mount retaining walls and Roman Aelia Capitolina, Emperor Constantine's Church of the Holy Sepulchre (335 CE), Umayyad Caliph ʿAbd al-Malik's Dome of the Rock (691/692 CE) and al-Aqsa Mosque, Crusader Latin Kingdom monuments, Mamluk madrasas, and Suleiman the Magnificent's 1537–1541 city walls.
evidence.limits: Long continuous stratified occupation leaves overlapping urban sanctuaries above ancient bedrock ridges.
evidence.dateBasis: Monuments carrying exact Roman, Umayyad (72 AH / 691–692 CE), Mamluk, and Ottoman builder inscriptions.

evidence.title: Baghdad (Madīnat al-Salām, Iraq): Abbasid Round City, House of Wisdom, 1258 siege & Ottoman Vilayet
evidence.summary: Founded by Caliph al-Manṣūr in 762 CE along a Tigris–Euphrates canal bend, circular Madīnat al-Salām drew scholars across Greek, Syriac, Sanskrit, and Persian traditions (the Abbasid Translation Movement under Hārūn al-Rashīd and al-Maʾmūn) and founded institutions like the Mustansiriya Madrasa (1227 CE), enduring Hulagu Khan's destructive 1258 siege and Safavid–Ottoman borderland rule through 1900.
evidence.limits: Al-Mansur's original West Bank Round City lies buried beneath modern urban districts; medieval architectural survival concentrates in East Baghdad (Mustansiriya, Abbasid Palace).
evidence.dateBasis: 762 CE foundation annals (al-Tabari/al-Khatib), 1227 CE Mustansiriya inscription, and 1258 Ilkhanid conquest records.

evidence.title: al-Aḥsāʾ & Qatif (Eastern Arabia, Saudi Arabia): artesian palm oasis, Qarmatians, Uyunids & Ottoman al-Hasa
evidence.summary: Fed by warm artesian karst springs supporting 2.5 million date palms along the Gulf edge, al-Aḥsāʾ served as headquarters of the egalitarian Qarmatian polity (founded 899 CE by Abū Saʿīd al-Jannābī, striking famously into Mecca in 930 CE), followed by the indigenous Uyunid (1076–1253), Usfurid, and Jabrid Arab emirates (Jawatha Mosque ruins), Ottoman Eyalet of Lahsa (1550–1670), and Banu Khalid confederation.
evidence.limits: Qarmatian accounts originate chiefly from hostile Baghdad chronicles alongside surviving numismatics and oasis archaeology.
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO al-Ahsa oasis synthesis, numismatic chronicles, and Ottoman–Arab Gulf archives.

evidence.title: Ṣanʿāʾ, Zabid & Aden (Yemen): tower-house metropolis, Zaydi Imamate, Rasulids & Red Sea coffee hub
evidence.summary: Highland Zaydi Imams (from 897 CE at Ṣaʿda and Ṣanʿāʾ), coastal Ziyadid/Najahid dynasties at Zabid (a university hub famed for algebra pioneer al-Khwārizmī connections and Shafi'i/Hanafi madrasas), the scholarly Rasulid Sultanate (1229–1454 CE, producing astronomical, agricultural, and maritime almanacs across Aden and Ta'izz), and Ottoman–British–Yemeni Aden made Yemen the Red Sea's agricultural and mocha coffee powerhouse.
evidence.limits: Dense multi-storey mud-brick/brick architecture at UNESCO Sana'a overlays pre-Islamic Sabaic stones.
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO Old Sana'a and Zabid documentation alongside surviving Rasulid royal treatises.

evidence.title: Isfahan, Shiraz & Tabriz (Iran): Buyid, Seljuk, Ilkhanid & Safavid imperial capitals (934–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Adjacent to the Arab world across the Zagros and Persian Gulf, Buyid Shiraz/Rayy, Seljuk Isfahan (Great Mosque's four-iwan dome innovation under Niẓām al-Mulk, 1080s), Ilkhanid Tabriz/Sultaniyya, and Shah ʿAbbās I's Safavid imperial capital at Isfahan (Naqsh-e Jahan Square, 1598 CE) anchored Persianate statecraft, Twelver Shi'i scholarship, Armenian Julfa trade diasporas, and Gulf–Eurasian silk exchanges through Qajar Iran (1900 CE).
evidence.limits: Represents the major Iranian urban triad complementing earlier Achaemenid Persepolis.
evidence.dateBasis: Dated Seljuk brick vaults, Ilkhanid waqf deeds, and 1598–1629 CE Safavid square inscriptions.

evidence.title: Sohar, Nizwa & Muscat (Oman): Abbasid port, Ibadi Imamate & Omani Indian Ocean Empire (750–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: From Abbasid-era maritime emporium at Sohar (celebrated by Arab geographers as the gateway to China alongside Siraf) and the enduring interior Ibadi Imamate centered at Nizwa and Rustaq, Oman's Yaʿāriba dynasty expelled the Portuguese from Muscat in 1650 and built a transoceanic maritime state under the Āl Bū Saʿīd linking Muscat, Gwadar, Mombasa, and Zanzibar across the 18th–19th centuries.
evidence.limits: Coordinates anchor Muscat harbor while maritime capital power alternated between Rustaq, Muscat, and Zanzibar (until the 1861 partition).
evidence.dateBasis: Arabic maritime geography, Ibadi Rustaq–Nizwa chronicles, and 1650/18th–19th-century Muscat treaties.

evidence.title: Diriyah (At-Turaif) & Riyadh (Wadi Ḥanīfah, Saudi Arabia): First & Second Saudi States (1446–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Founded by Māniʿ al-Muraydī along the limestone wadi cliffs of Wadi Ḥanīfah in 1446 CE, Diriyah grew into the mud-brick Najdi oasis capital of the First Saudi State (1727 / 1744 Diriyah Pact uniting Muhammad ibn Saud and reformer Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab), expanding across nearly the entire Arabian Peninsula before Ibrahim Pasha's Ottoman–Egyptian siege razed At-Turaif in 1818, followed by Turki ibn 'Abdallah re-establishing the Second Saudi State at nearby Riyadh (1824–1891 CE).
evidence.limits: At-Turaif mud-brick palaces experienced severe ruin after 1818 prior to late-20th-century conservation; Najdi town coalitions shifted dynamically under Rashidi Ha'il rivalry in the late 19th century.
evidence.dateBasis: Najdi chronicles (Ibn Ghannam, Ibn Bishr), 1818 siege reports, and UNESCO At-Turaif architectural surveys.

evidence.title: Ahichchhatra & Hastinapura (Upper Ganga–Yamuna Doab): Painted Grey Ware & Early Vedic–Kuru transition
evidence.summary: Between the decline of Late Harappan towns and Second Urbanization cities, Painted Grey Ware (PGW) villages and nucleated iron-using settlements across Punjab and the upper Ganga–Yamuna Doab—including excavated levels at Hastinapura, Ahichchhatra, Bhagwanpura, and Atranjikhera—correspond geographically with early Kuru and Panchala state formation recorded in later Vedic and epic traditions.
evidence.limits: Pottery horizons and oral Vedic hymns belong to different evidentiary registers; archaeology shows gradual settlement growth and early iron metallurgy without literal confirmation of every epic narrative.
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon and TL chronology of Painted Grey Ware strata across the upper Ganga–Yamuna Doab.

evidence.title: Rajagriha (Rajgir) & Vaishali (Bihar): Sixteen Mahajanapadas & Shramana urbanism (c. 600–320 BCE)
evidence.summary: Driven by wet-rice agriculture, iron ploughs/axes, Northern Black Polished Ware, and silver punch-marked coinage, sixteen competing kingdoms and oligarchic *gana-sanghas* (*Mahajanapadas*) consolidated across northern India—led by Magadha inside its 40-km stone mountain walls at Rajagriha and the Licchavi republic at Vaishali, providing the direct social setting for Gautama Buddha and Mahavira.
evidence.limits: Chronology for Nanda and earlier Magadhan kings balances archaeological NBPW dates with later Buddhist/Jain chronicles (often adjusted around ~486/400 BCE nirvana debates).
evidence.dateBasis: Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) excavations, silver karshapana coinage, and Rajgir cyclopean fortification surveys.

evidence.title: Pataliputra (Patna) & Sarnath: Mauryan Empire & Ashoka's continent-wide rock/pillar edicts (321–185 BCE)
evidence.summary: Founded by Chandragupta Maurya at the Ganga–Son confluence and famed via Megasthenes' *Indika*, Pataliputra's 80-pillared sandstone hall anchored South Asia's first pan-subcontinental empire (stretching from Kandahar to Karnataka). Emperor Ashoka inscribed public moral-and-administrative *Dhamma* edicts in Brahmi, Kharoshthi, Greek, and Aramaic on polished Chunar sandstone pillars (crowned by Sarnath's four-lion capital) and living boulders.
evidence.limits: Provincial autonomy varied widely outside core metropolitan Gangetic and resource hubs.
evidence.dateBasis: Excavations at Kumrahar (Pataliputra), synchronisms with Hellenistic kings named in Ashoka's Major Rock Edict XIII (~256 BCE).

evidence.title: Sisupalgarh, Dhauli & Udayagiri (Kalinga / Odisha): fortified grid city & Kharavela inscription (300 BCE–300 CE)
evidence.summary: Site of Ashoka's watershed Kalinga conquest (c. 261 BCE, openly mourned in the Dhauli/Jaugada Special Edicts), coastal Odisha later rose as an independent maritime kingdom under Mahameghavahana King Kharavela—chronicled in the Hathigumpha cave inscription—centered at perfectly square rectilinear ramparts and laterite gateways excavated at Sisupalgarh.
evidence.limits: Dating of Kharavela shifts between late 2nd/1st c. BCE depending on paleographic synchronisms with Satavahana kings.
evidence.dateBasis: Mauryan–post-Mauryan rock edicts at Dhauli, Hathigumpha cave epigraphy, and geophysical–excavation grid plans at Sisupalgarh.

evidence.title: Sanchi, Vidisha & Bharhut (Central India): Great Stupa *toranas* & Besnagar Heliodorus Pillar (250 BCE–500 CE)
evidence.summary: Originating with an Ashokan brick stupa above the commercial hub of Vidisha, Sanchi's Great Stupa was encased in stone and encircled under Shunga and Satavahana guilds by four densely carved gateways (*toranas*) paid for by hundreds of ordinary lay donors named in Brahmi inscriptions—while nearby Besnagar preserves the ~113 BCE Heliodorus Pillar erected in honor of Vasudeva by a Greek ambassador from Taxila.
evidence.limits: Demonstrates pluralistic mercantile patronage across Buddhist monasticism, Bhagavata devotion, and Indo-Greek diplomacy.
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO Sanchi architectural phases and Brahmi donative/Vasudeva inscriptions.

evidence.title: Mathura (Yamuna Plain, UP): Southern Kushan capital, Bactrian–Sanskrit crossroads & sculpture ateliers (100 BCE–350 CE)
evidence.summary: Serving alongside Purushapura (Peshawar) as twin imperial center of the Kushan Empire under Kanishka I (c. 127–150 CE), Sonkh and Mathura sandstone workshops produced both royal headless dynastic portraits (the *devakula* at Mat), early anthropomorphic Buddha/Bodhisattva and Jain Tirthankara images, Vaishnava/Shaiva icons, and dated Saka-era donative records linking Central Asian steppe empires with the Gangetic plains.
evidence.limits: Debate over the exact start year of Kanishka's era has narrowed around c. 127 CE based on the Rabatak inscription and numismatics.
evidence.dateBasis: Kushan regnal inscriptions in spotted Sikri sandstone and stratified urban excavations at Sonkh.

evidence.title: Pratishthana (Paithan) & Amaravati–Nagarjunakonda (Deccan): Satavahana–Ikshvaku inland trade & Roman bullion
evidence.summary: Bridging the Western Ghats rock-cut cave monasteries (Karle, Bhaja, Nasik—endowed by Queen Naganika and Gautamiputra Satakarni) with Krishna-river Palnad limestone stupas at Amaravati and Ikshvaku Nagarjunakonda, Satavahana polities taxed trans-Deccan cotton, agate, and iron exports flowing into Mediterranean ships at Barygaza and Arikamedu.
evidence.limits: Early Satavahana regnal chronology fluctuates between 2nd-c. and 1st-c. BCE start estimates.
evidence.dateBasis: Cave donative epigraphy, ship-motif Satavahana lead/potin coinage, and Krishna Valley monastic excavations.

evidence.title: Prayāga (Allahabad), Sarnath & Ujjain: Gupta Empire, Iron Pillar & Sanskrit scientific renaissance (320–550 CE)
evidence.summary: Starting from the middle Ganga basin under Chandragupta I (319/320 CE Gupta Era), Samudragupta's Allahabad Pillar *prashasti* mapped a pan-Indian tributary order while Chandragupta II pushed west into Saka-held Malwa/Ujjain. Gupta-Vakataka patronage witnessed Kalidasa's literature, Sarnath and Deogarh classical sculpture, decimal place-value mathematical–astronomical synthesis (Aryabhata, *Aryabhatiya* 499 CE), and the corrosion-resistant Mehrauli Iron Pillar.
evidence.limits: Rather than an over-centralized bureaucracy, Gupta authority operated largely through land-grant *agrahara* charters and allied tributary courts like the Vakatakas.
evidence.dateBasis: Gupta Era (epoch 319/320 CE) copperplate grants, Allahabad Pillar inscription, and Aryabhata's 499 CE astronomical epoch.

evidence.title: Nālandā Mahāvihāra, Bodh Gaya & Vikramashila (Bihar–Bengal): International monastic universities & Pāla art (427–1200 CE)
evidence.summary: Founded under Gupta ruler Kumaragupta I (c. 427 CE) and expanded by Harsha and the Buddhist Pāla Empire of Bengal–Bihar (750–1161 CE), UNESCO-listed Nālandā Mahāvihāra operated as a residential international university endowed by two hundred revenue-paying villages (and even Srivijayan king Balaputradeva of Sumatra), hosting masters Dharmapala, Shantarakshita, Atisha, Xuanzang, and Yijing while radiating bronzes and manuscripts to Tibet and Java.
evidence.limits: Raids around 1200 CE dealt heavy blows to Bihar monasteries, though localized monastic scholarly activity lingered decades afterward.
evidence.dateBasis: Gupta–Pala royal clay seals excavated in Nalanda Monasteries 1–11 and Xuanzang's 7th-century records.

evidence.title: Kannauj (Kānyakubja, UP): Emperor Harsha & Gurjara-Pratihāra–Rāṣṭrakūṭa–Pāla Tripartite Contest (606–1018 CE)
evidence.summary: Under Pushyabhuti ruler Harshavardhana (r. 606–647 CE, documented by court poet Banabhatta and pilgrim Xuanzang), Kannauj displaced Pataliputra as North India's premier imperial capital. For two centuries afterward (c. 780–950 CE), Kannauj became the supreme geopolitical prize in the Tripartite Struggle fought between the Gurjara-Pratiharas of Rajasthan/Malwa, Palas of Bengal, and Rashtrakutas of the Deccan until Ghaznavid raids in 1018 CE.
evidence.limits: Modern Kannauj covers much of the ancient mound; textual–inscriptional sources reconstruct most political turns.
evidence.dateBasis: Harsha Era (606 CE) inscriptions, Gwalior Mihira Bhoja Prashasti, and 1018 CE chronicle accounts.

evidence.title: Kanchipuram, Mamallapuram & Madurai (Tamil Nadu): Pallava rock-cut architecture, Bhakti & Pandya guilds (300–900 CE)
evidence.summary: From their learned capital at Kanchipuram and granite port at Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram), the Pallavas—notably Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I (630–668 CE)—pioneered rock-cut *mandapas*, the monolithic Five *Rathas*, the colossal *Descent of the Ganges* relief, and the structural Shore Temple looking toward the Bay of Bengal, parallel with Madurai's Pandya revival and the vernacular Tamil Shiva/Vishnu Bhakti hymns of the Nayanars and Alvars.
evidence.limits: Monument attributions combine Sanskrit/Tamil Pallava *biruda* inscriptions with architectural seriation.
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO Mahabalipuram architectural dossier and Pallava/Pandya copperplate and cliff inscriptions.

evidence.title: Badami, Aihole, Pattadakal & Manyakheta (Karnataka): Chalukya & Rāṣṭrakūṭa synthesis (543–973 CE)
evidence.summary: From cliff-carved cave shrines at Badami and Aihole's architectural laboratory, Early Chalukya king Pulakeshin II halted Harsha at the Narmada (c. 618 CE, Aihole Inscription), while Chalukya queens Lokamahadevi and Trailokyamahadevi built the UNESCO-listed Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna temples at Pattadakal (c. 740 CE) deliberately fusing northern *Nagara* and southern *Dravida* stone towers—inspiring their Rashtrakuta successors' Kailasa monolith at Ellora.
evidence.limits: Earlier Chalukyas were succeeded in the 750s by Rashtrakutas based at Manyakheta and later the Western Kalyani Chalukyas.
evidence.dateBasis: Dated Shaka-era temple foundation inscriptions (e.g., Badami Cliff 543 CE, Aihole 634 CE) and Pattadakal royal records.

evidence.title: Anuradhapura, Sigiriya & Polonnaruwa (Sri Lanka): hydraulic tank kingdoms & monastic chronicles (377 BCE–1236 CE)
evidence.summary: Sustained by cascading dry-zone artificial lakes (*wewa* reservoirs) and stone sluices engineered from early historic times, UNESCO-listed Anuradhapura flourished for 1,300 years alongside brick *dagobas* (Jetavanaramaya once among the ancient world's tallest brick structures), Kashyapa's 5th-c. rock citadel frescoes at Sigiriya, the Pali *Mahavamsa* historical chronicle, and later Polonnaruwa's Parakramabahu I hydraulic synthesis.
evidence.limits: Early Anuradhapura traditional chronicle dates are steadily calibrated against Brahmi cave epigraphy and core-drilled reservoir sediment.
evidence.dateBasis: Early Brahmi donor inscriptions, Sigiriya graffiti verses, and Anuradhapura citadel trench radiocarbon dates.

evidence.title: Khajuraho, Rānī-ki-Vāv (Patan) & Konark (900–1300 CE): Rajput, Solanki & Eastern Ganga stone engineering
evidence.summary: Before and alongside northern sultanate rule, regional dynasties raised some of India's most intricate masonry monuments: Chandela sandstone *Nagara* spires at Khajuraho (c. 950–1050 CE), Solanki Queen Udayamati's seven-storey subterranean sculpted stepwell at Rānī-ki-Vāv, Patan (11th c. Gujarat), and Eastern Ganga ruler Narasimhadeva I's 24-wheeled chariot Sun Temple at Konark, Odisha (c. 1250 CE).
evidence.limits: Khajuraho represents one cluster; coordinates mark the Khajuraho UNESCO complex.
evidence.dateBasis: Vikrama Samvat temple foundation records and Eastern Ganga royal copperplates.

evidence.title: Delhi Sultanate Capitals (Qutb Minar, Siri, Tughlaqabad & Lodi Gardens, 1192–1526 CE)
evidence.summary: Successive Delhi Sultanate capitals (Qutb Minar/Lal Kot, Alauddin Khalji's Siri that repelled Chagatai Mongol invasions, Muhammad bin Tughluq's Tughlaqabad/Jahanpanah where Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta served as judge from 1334–1341, Firoz Shah Kotla, and the Lodi tomb-gardens) forged Indo-Islamic arches, corbel-to-true vaults, paper bureaucracy, Persian-Sanskrit translations, and northern defenses until Babur's 1526 First Battle of Panipat.
evidence.limits: Delhi's imperial reach expanded and contracted sharply between Alauddin Khalji / Muhammad Tughluq peaks and Timur's 1398 sack.
evidence.dateBasis: 1192 CE Tarain/Qutb foundation epigraphy, Moroccan traveler and court chronicles, and standing Delhi Sultanate monuments.

evidence.title: Gaur, Pandua & Sonargaon (Bengal Sultanate, 1204–1576 CE): terracotta mosques, muslin & Ming envoys
evidence.summary: From 1352 to 1576 CE, the independent Bengal Sultanate centered at Pandua (Adina Mosque, 1375 CE), Gaur (curved-*chala* terracotta brick mosques), and riverine Sonargaon coined vast silver *tankas*, exchanged diplomatic embassies and a famous Malindi giraffe with Ming Yongle/Zheng He's fleets (recorded by Ma Huan in 1432), exported fine Dacca/Sonargaon cotton muslins, and nurtured early Bengali literary translation alongside Vaishnava Bhakti (Chaitanya).
evidence.limits: Ganga river shifts eroded parts of historic Gaur; surviving brick-and-glazed-tile monuments concentrate along the Malda borderland.
evidence.dateBasis: Dated Bengal Sultanate silver tankas, Adina Mosque 776 AH inscription, and Ming court records.

evidence.title: Charaideo Maidams, Garhgaon & Rangpur (Ahom Kingdom, Assam, 1228–1826 CE): 600-year Brahmaputra polity
evidence.summary: Crossing the Patkai mountains in 1228 CE under Sukaphaa, the Ahom Kingdom governed the Upper Brahmaputra Valley for six centuries through the *paik* labor–militia system, chronicled in Tai–Ahom and Assamese *Buranji* histories, constructing UNESCO-listed hemispherical royal vaulted burial mounds (*maidams*) at Charaideo and amphitheater palaces at Garhgaon/Rangpur while repeatedly repelling Mughal invasions—culminating in Lachit Borphukan's 1671 naval victory at Saraighat.
evidence.limits: Ahom state structure underwent major socio-religious transitions incorporating Assamese language and Vaishnava satra institutions.
evidence.dateBasis: Buranji royal chronicles, Ahom coins/copperplates, and UNESCO Charaideo Maidam stratigraphy.

evidence.title: Calicut (Kozhikode), Cochin & Goa (Malabar–Konkan Coast, 1300–1800 CE): Spice Emporia & Maritime Encounter
evidence.summary: Under the Zamorins (*Samuthiri*) of Calicut, Kerala's black-pepper ports hosted thriving Mappila Muslim, Jewish (Cochin), St. Thomas Christian, Arab Karimi, and Chinese trading guilds—welcoming Ibn Battuta, Wang Dayuan, and Zheng He (who died near Calicut in 1433) long before Vasco da Gama's 1498 arrival and Afonso de Albuquerque's 1510 capture of Goa initiated armed Portuguese *cartaz* passes and Dutch VOC–Travancore pepper diplomacy (1741 Battle of Colachel).
evidence.limits: European coastal forts controlled selected sea lanes without ruling the agrarian interior during the 16th–17th centuries.
evidence.dateBasis: Arabic/Chinese navigation manuals (Ibn Majid, Ma Huan), Kerala temple/port chronicles, and 1498/1510/1741 dates.

evidence.title: Amritsar & Lahore (Punjab): Harmandir Sahib, Guru Granth Sahib (1604), Khalsa (1699) & Sikh Empire (1577–1849 CE)
evidence.summary: Excavated in 1577 CE under Guru Ram Das, Amritsar's Sacred Pool (*Amrit Sarovar*) and four-doored Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) became Sikhism's spiritual center where Guru Arjan compiled the *Adi Granth* in 1604 CE. Following Guru Gobind Singh's creation of the Khalsa in 1699 CE and confederated *Misl* resistance, Maharaja Ranjit Singh forged a modernized multi-faith Sikh Empire centered at Lahore and Amritsar (1799–1849 CE) before British annexation.
evidence.limits: Golden Temple gilt cladding dates largely to Ranjit Singh's early 19th-century rebuilding over 16th–18th-century foundations.
evidence.dateBasis: 1604 Adi Granth compilation, 1699 Anandpur Khalsa, 1799 Lahore capture, and 1849 Punjab annexation treaties.

evidence.title: Calcutta, Bombay, Madras & the 1857 Uprising: EIC Transition to Crown Rail & Early Nationalism (1757–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Following East India Company military–fiscal takeover from Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) through the 1818 defeat of the Maratha Confederacy, deep agrarian revenue extraction, deindustrialization pressures, and the 1857 Revolt (spanning Meerut, Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, and Jhansi) ended Company rule for the British Crown Raj (1858)—while new print public spheres, railways, universities, and social reform movements founded early nationalist institutions in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras through 1900.
evidence.limits: Economic impact differed sharply between irrigated canal zones, deindustrialized Bengal weavers, and princely states (covering ~40% of the subcontinent).
evidence.dateBasis: East India Company & Crown treaties (1757–1858), decennial censuses (1871–1891), and 1885 Congress founding archives.

waves.title: Arabian Incense Road: Dhofar & Maʾrib via Qaryat al-Fāw, Najran, Dedan & Hegra to Gaza/Petra
waves.summary: Multi-stage camel caravan system connecting Dhofari frankincense groves and Sabaean–Himyarite highlands through Qaryat al-Fāw, Dadān, Taymāʾ, and Hegra to Petra and Mediterranean ports.
waves.limits: Incense was transported in segmented tribal relays rather than by single end-to-end caravans.

waves.title: Darb Zubaydah & Syrian/Red Sea Hajj Network: Kufa, Damascus & Jeddah into the Hijaz (750–1900 CE)
waves.summary: Permanent water-engineered pilgrim and scholarly exchange trunk uniting Iraq, Najd reservoirs, Medina, Mecca, and the Red Sea port of Jeddah.
waves.limits: Only the primary Iraqi Darb Zubaydah–Hejaz spine is plotted here; complementary Egyptian and Syrian tracks are marked at coastal and oasis junctions.

waves.title: Uttarāpatha & Dakṣiṇāpatha Subcontinental Trunk Corridors (Taxila–Pataliputra–Deccan–Kanchipuram)
waves.summary: Ancient India's northern Gangetic highway (*Uttarāpatha*) linked via Vidisha/Paithan down the *Dakṣiṇāpatha* southern highway to Deccan monastic trade caves and Tamil capitals.
waves.limits: Generalized alignment across well-attested Mauryan–Satavahana–Gupta–Chalukya junction cities.

waves.title: Monsoon Indian Ocean Linkages: Gujarat & Malabar via Sri Lanka & Coromandel to Bengal & SE Asia
waves.summary: Seasonal southwest/northeast monsoon sailing circuit uniting Gulf of Khambhat textiles, Malabar pepper, Sri Lankan pearls/cinnamon, Chola Coromandel bronze & guilds, Bengal muslins, and Strait of Malacca entrepôts.
waves.limits: Schematic coastal sea-lane connecting historic harbors.
